l6-icm: ICM (Independent Chip Model) is a mathematical model that calculates the real value ($EV) of chips in tournaments. Unlike cash games, chip value in tournaments is not linear — your first chip is worth more than your last chip.
Core concept: in tournaments Chip EV ≠ $EV. 10,000 chips are not worth 2 × 5,000 chips.

In cash games, each 1BB has a fixed value (e.g. $1). But in tournaments:
- Doubling your chips doesn't double your prize
- Losing half your chips costs you more than half your expected prize
- Survival itself has value (the prize ladder)

1. Big stacks are worth less than their chip share (diminishing marginal value)
   Example: a player holding 50% of chips may have only 40% $EV

2. Short stacks are worth more than their chip share (survival value)
   Example: a player holding 10% of chips may have 15% $EV

3. Medium stacks should avoid clashing with big stacks on the bubble
   Because the loss from elimination far exceeds the gain from doubling

Bubble Factor measures the strength of ICM pressure:
- Bubble Factor = 1: no ICM pressure (like cash games)
- Bubble Factor > 1: ICM pressure exists (tournaments)
- Highest on the bubble, reaching 1.5-2.0

The higher the Bubble Factor, the tighter your calling range should be.

### Minimal example: SNG prize structure
Assume a 4-player SNG: 1st=$50, 2nd=$30, 3rd=$20, 4th=$0
Chip distribution: A=40BB, B=30BB, C=20BB, D=10BB

**Step 1: each player's win probability ≈ chip share**
- P(A wins) = 40/(40+30+20+10) = 40%

**Step 2: probability of two-player final**
- P(A & B finish top 2) = combination calculation...
- P(A 2nd) = Σ(P(X 1st) × P(A 2nd | X 1st))

**Step 3: final $EV**
- A's $EV = Σ(P(i wins at position j) × prize_j)
- = 0.4×$50 + 0.32×$30 + 0.2×$20 = $36.6

That means 40BB of chips has an expected value of $36.6 in this SNG

### Definition and formula
Bubble Factor = required equity for call / required equity in a cash game

### Example
- In a cash game facing a 50% pot bet, you need 27% equity to call
- In ICM, BF can reach 1.5-2.0 (higher in extreme cases)
- Actual required equity = 27% × 1.5 = 40.5%

This means on the bubble you must fold with a wider range, even hands you'd call in cash games.

Bubble period strategy adjustments:
- Tighten the calling range: need stronger hands to call all-ins
- Keep or widen the push range: exploit opponents' ICM fear
- Big stacks can push short stacks with wider ranges
- Short stacks should seek the best shove spot, not passively wait
ICM is the cornerstone of tournament strategy. Once you understand ICM, you'll see why you fold AQ to an all-in on the bubble and why big stacks can "bully" short stacks.

ICM minimal example (4-player SNG, prizes 50/30/20):
Chip distribution: A=5000, B=3000, C=1500, D=500 (total 10000)

A's $EV calculation (simplified):
First-place probability ≈ 5000/10000 = 50%, prize $50
Second-place probability ≈ combination calculation...
$EV ≈ 0.5×50 + 0.3×30 + 0.15×20 + 0.05×0 = $36.5

Bubble Factor:
BF = required equity to call / required equity in cash
On the bubble, BF can reach 1.5-2.0, meaning you need about 1.5-2x the equity to call

Core conclusion: doubling chips doesn't double the prize. 5000 chips' $EV is not 2 × 2500's.

Theory reference: the full derivation of the ICM recursive algorithm and the Bubble Factor formula is in Theory Academy T9 Chapter 2 "ICM Theory", including $EV calculation methods for multi-player SNGs and the mathematical foundation of tournament strategy.

Counter-intuitive: doubling chips doesn't double your prize. In the ICM model, chip marginal value diminishes — going from 500 to 1000 matters more than from 5000 to 5500. That's why short stacks should be more aggressive on the bubble and big stacks more conservative.
l6-pushfold:
When your stack drops below 15BB, consider entering Push/Fold mode:
- < 15BB: start considering push/fold
- < 10BB: must use push/fold strategy
- < 8BB: look for push opportunities from almost any position

Reason: when chips are too shallow, postflop playability drops sharply, and getting 3-bet after an open-raise is awkward.
Push/Fold core: replace open-raises with all-ins to maximize fold equity and avoid postflop decisions.

Nash equilibrium is the optimal-strategy concept from game theory. In Push/Fold spots:
- Push range: a range that makes opponent calls unprofitable
- Call range: a range with +EV against the opponent's push range

In practice you should:
- vs tight opponents: push wider than Nash
- vs loose opponents: push tighter than Nash

Push ranges at 10BB:
- BTN push: about 40-45% (any Ax, any pair, K8s+, Q9s+, J9s+, T9s, 98s)
- SB push: about 50-55% (wider, only BB remains)

Push ranges at 15BB:
- BTN push: about 25-30% (tighter, chips still have postflop value)
- SB push: about 35-40%

Push ranges at 8BB:
- BTN push: about 50%+ (very wide)
- Any position: look for push opportunities
BB's Calling Range vs a Push

BB's call range vs a push depends on:
1. Opponent position: BTN push is much wider than UTG push
2. Opponent stack: short stacks push wider
3. ICM pressure: tighter call range on the bubble

General rules:
- vs BTN 10BB push: call about 30-35% (any pair, A2s+, K9s+, QJs)
- vs UTG 10BB push: call about 15-20% (77+, ATs+, KQs)

Cash games:
- Push/Fold rarely used (except extremely short)
- Can use min-raise to keep postflop playability

Tournaments:
- ICM pressure widens push ranges (opponents call tighter)
- Push ranges can be wider than Nash on the bubble
- Push wider when final-table pay jumps are big
Push/Fold is the core short-stack skill in tournaments. Remember: at 10BB the BTN can push 40%+ of hands — much wider than most people's intuition.

ICM Bubble Factor definition:
BF = required equity to call / required equity in cash

Explanation: on the bubble, survival weight > immediate EV, so the Bubble Factor is usually 1.5-3.0x. You need higher equity to call because folding might mean survival ($EV > 0).

Example: 4-player SNG bubble (prizes 50%/30%/20%)
- Chip distribution: you 40%, MP 35%, CO 20%, BTN 5%
- Your $EV(fold) = 35% (securing 2nd)
- Your $EV(call, win) = 50%
- Your $EV(call, lose) = 0
- Break-even: 35 <= p×50% + (1-p)×0 → p >= 70%
- In cash you'd only need: pot odds (e.g. 43%)
- Bubble Factor ≈ 70%/43% ≈ 1.6x

Nash Push/Fold equilibrium ranges (10BB spot):
SB Push range (vs BB):
- All pairs 22+
- All Ax
- All suited Kx
- KTo+
- Q9s+, QTo+
- J9s+, JTo
- T9s, 98s
- Total about 70-80% of hands

BB Call range (vs SB Push):
- All pairs 44+
- A7o+, A4s+
- KTo+, K9s+
- QJo, QTs+
- Total about 35-40% of hands

Break-even calculation:
BB calls 10BB to win 12BB (incl. blinds)
Required equity = 9/(9+12) ≈ 43%
Theory reference: the full derivation of Nash Push/Fold equilibrium ranges is in Theory Academy T9 Chapter 2 "ICM Theory". Tournament ICM pressure and Push/Fold decisions are closely related.

Counter-intuitive: UTG's push range at 10BB is nearly wide open (about 70-80%), not "tight". Many players think short-stacked UTG should only push strong hands, but Nash equilibrium shows UTG at 10BB can push an extremely wide range — because folding means blinds get eaten, while pushing captures fold equity.
l6-bubble:
The bubble is the stage with only 1-3 eliminations left before the money. For example:
- 100 players, top 15 get paid
- When only 16-18 remain, it's the bubble

This is the stage with the highest ICM pressure, because:
- Eliminating 1-3 more players enters the money
- Elimination = zero prize
- Entering the money = at least min-cash
The bubble is the stage with the highest ICM pressure in a tournament, and the stage where big stacks profit the most.

If you're one of the top 3 big stacks:

1. Aggressive pressure
   - Open wide (40-50%)
   - 3-bet wide (especially vs medium stacks)
   - Exploit medium stacks' ICM fear

2. Target selection
   - Attack medium stacks first (they fear elimination most)
   - Short stacks may "fight back" (nothing left to lose)

3. Position exploitation
   - Apply maximum pressure from BTN/CO
   - Medium stacks in the blinds face the toughest decisions

If you're a medium stack:

1. Avoid clashing with big stacks
   - When a big stack opens, 3-bet/call with a tighter range
   - Don't "prove yourself" — survival first

2. Pressure short stacks
   - Open/3-bet wide against short stacks
   - Short stacks need very tight calling ranges

3. Position awareness
   - Play tighter behind big stacks
   - Play wider behind short stacks

If you're a short stack (< 10BB):

1. Seek the best shove spot
   - Push when early positions fold to you (max fold equity)
   - Avoid pushing behind big stacks

2. Don't passively wait
   - Pushing below 5BB is too late
   - Pushing at 10-15BB still has fold equity

3. Hand selection
   - Prefer hands with blockers (Ax, Kx)
   - Avoid "dominated" hands (KJ, QT etc.)
Strategy Shift After the Bubble Bursts

After the bubble bursts (someone is eliminated into the money):

1. ICM pressure drops sharply
   - Everyone has min-cashed
   - The next target is a higher finish

2. Ranges widen
   - Short stacks can "go for it"
   - Medium stacks no longer fear so much

3. Strategy adjustments
   - Return closer to cash-game play
   - Still watch for pay jumps
The bubble is a big stack's "money printer". If you're short, don't be afraid to push at 10-15BB — waiting until 5BB is too late.
l6-finaltable: The Impact of Final Table Payout Structure

Final tables (usually 9 or 6 players) have big pay jumps:
- 9th: $1,000
- 8th: $1,500
- 7th: $2,200
- ...
- 1st: $20,000

This means:
- Every elimination has a significant prize jump
- ICM pressure is still strong at the final table
- Big stacks can exploit pay jumps to apply pressure
Final-table strategy core: adjust dynamically based on pay jumps and chip distribution — don't "play one style all the way".

Adjust strategy by table chip distribution:

1. You're a big stack (top 2-3)
   - Apply pressure with wide opens/3-bets
   - Exploit medium stacks' ICM fear
   - Goal: accumulate chips, chase 1st place

2. You're a medium stack
   - Avoid clashing with big stacks
   - Pressure short stacks
   - Goal: survive, wait for a better spot

3. You're a short stack
   - Seek the best shove spot
   - Don't passively wait
   - Goal: double up or bust

When to steal:
- Blinds are big (relative to stacks)
- Opponents are tight (high fold-to-steal)
- You're in position (BTN/CO)

Steal range:
- BTN: 40-50% (any Ax, any pair, most suited hands)
- CO: 30-40%

Steal size:
- Min-raise (2-2.2x) is most common
- Gives opponents the worst odds
- Reduces your own risk

Re-stealing is 3-betting all-in from the blinds against a stealer:

When to re-steal:
- The opponent steals often (open > 40%)
- You have 15-25BB (too little = no fold equity, too much = wasteful)
- You have blockers (Ax, Kx)

Hand selection:
- Ax: block the opponent's Ax combos
- Suited hands: postflop playability
- Avoid "dominated" hands (KJ, QT)

Heads-Up is the final stage of a tournament:

1. Extremely wide ranges
   - SB (BTN) opens 70-80%
   - BB defends 60-70%

2. Aggression is key
   - Passive = lose
   - Active pressure wins blinds

3. Adaptability
   - Observe opponent tendencies
   - Tight opponent → steal more
   - Loose opponent → value bet more
The final table is the most important stage of a tournament. Remember: big stacks should exploit pay jumps with pressure, short stacks should actively seek push opportunities.
l6-bounty: In Progressive Knockout (PKO) tournaments, every player carries a bounty. Eliminating an opponent awards half their bounty; the other half is added to your own head. This completely changes strategy.
Bounties make "eliminating" valuable in itself. When covering an opponent, your calling/raising range should be wider than in a normal tournament, because there's bounty value beyond the pot.

• When covering short stacks: significantly widen your calling/raising range (bounty value is high)
• When covered: play normally — don't get "excited" by opponents' 3-Bets
• When your bounty is big: opponents will raise at you more aggressively
• Calculate "bounty-adjusted odds":
  Effective odds = (pot + opponent bounty/2) : call amount
The most common PKO mistake is completely ignoring bounty value (playing too tight) or over-chasing bounties (shoving garbage hands). Balance is key.

Bounty tournament $EV adjustment formula:
Effective bounty value = fixed bounty × elimination probability
Adjusted call required equity = original required equity × (1 - bounty discount factor)

Example: bounty $20, opponent chips 5000, total chips 50000
Elimination probability = 5000/50000 = 10%
Bounty $EV contribution = 0.1 × $20 = $2

This means your calling range can widen about 5-10%, depending on bounty size and chip distribution

Theory reference: multiway equity dilution and bounty-tournament $EV adjustments are in Theory Academy T9 Chapter 3 "Multiway Pots and the GTO-Exploitation Unified Framework". Bounty strategy is ICM theory extended to a special format.

Counter-intuitive: against a big-bounty opponent you should actually tighten your calling range. Many think "big bounty means chase more aggressively", but mathematically a big-bounty opponent has a low elimination probability, so the bounty's $EV contribution is limited. Blindly chasing bounties leads to -EV calls.
